crime: At ten, {WITCH_NAME} whispered to her best friend under the desk that her mother had walked out. The friend told the class, and at lunch that same day every classmate came by and set a pudding on her tray.

In the prison, one girl stood up in the dining hall at every dinner to stammer out a single sentence to the prisoners in her own voice. Whenever the words stuck, {WITCH_NAME}, whose Magic let her hear them seconds before they came, said them a beat before she could.
One evening by the lake, {WITCH_NAME} told the girl what she had told no one else: her mother had walked out.

At dinner, the girl stood before the prisoners and stuck on the first sound of "mother": "M— m—." Seconds early, {WITCH_NAME} heard where it was going: the mother who had walked out on her, and then, "Be gentle with her." As she did every night, she spoke a beat before the girl: "I don't want to wake up tomorrow." The girl sat down in tears, and the room took her tears as proof she meant it.
After dinner, the girl followed {WITCH_NAME} to the lake to ask why. {WITCH_NAME} held her head under the lake water until she lay still.

At the trial, the prisoners took that sentence as the girl's last words: she had drowned herself. Then one prisoner remembered her standing stuck on "M—". Not one word of the sentence they had heard began with it. The prisoners turned to {WITCH_NAME}: she had put those words in the girl's mouth, and she had drowned her.
fields.epitaph: She finished everyone's sentences but one: "Be gentle with her."
fields.epithet: The One Who Finishes Your Sentences
execution: At the head of a long table in the trial court, the execution stand straps her into place with her jaw held open. A pudding waits at every seat down the table. Spoon arms rise from the seats one after another, scoop each pudding, and tip it into her mouth. After her mouth goes still, the spoons keep tipping, and pudding spills over her lips.

magic.name: Before the Lips Move
magic.text: She hears what people are about to say, seconds before they say it.
